newsitem.title: CHINA: Two China labour activists jailed for 3-1/2 years.
newsitem.headline: Two China labour activists jailed for 3-1/2 years.

text.p: A Chinese court has jailed two labour activists for 3-1/2 years each for conspiring to subvert the government in a long-delayed ruling denounced on Tuesday by an international human rights monitoring group.

A court in the southern boomtown of Shenzhen convicted Li Wen-ming and Guo Baosheng on May 30, the Hong Kong-based Information Centre of Human Rights and Democratic Movement in China said in a statement received in Beijing.
Li, 28, and Guo, 25, who have been in custody since 1994, are due to be released in November and December this year, respectively.
Li, a former magazine employee, and Guo, a former university student, were also deprived of their political rights for two years, the group said.
This means they cannot talk to foreign reporters or write for overseas publications for two years after their release from prison.
It was not known if they would appeal their convictions, which came days before the eighth anniversary of the bloody military crackdown on student-led demonstrations for democracy on June 4, 1989.
They could have been sentenced to death, Human Rights Watch, a New York-based group, said.
Their trial had ended last November, but the court dragged its feet and delayed sentencing until last month in violation of domestic law, Human Rights Watch said.
Court officials were not immediately available for comment.
Human Rights Watch condemned the sentences as a serious violation of international human rights standards.

"Li and Guo were guilty of nothing more than trying to educate Chinese migrant workers about their rights to organise and engage in collective bargaining in the workplace," said Sidney Jones, executive director of Human Rights Watch/Asia.
"They should never have been detained for a single day, let alone held incommunicado for two and a half years and then sentenced to further time in jail after a closed trial," she said.
Human Rights Watch said Li was suffering from acute kidney damage, but has been denied access to appropriate medical care and was in danger of losing one kidney.

"The symptoms are sufficiently grave that unless Li is permitted to receive immediate treatment, he may be in imminent danger of losing at least one kidney," Human Rights Watch said, quoting Chinese medical experts consulted recently by people close to Li's family.
Li's face was said to be badly swollen and he reportedly has difficulty in standing unaided, it said.

International human rights groups and Western governments have criticised Beijing for silencing dissidents in 1996 -- a year that saw members of the tiny pro-democracy movement jailed, intimidated or driven into exile.
China rejects criticism of human rights abuses as interference in its internal affairs, arguing that the right to the bare necessities of life is more important than political rights.
